https://aeon.co/essays/why-intellectual-.question: Can humility itself be an obstacle to understanding?
https://aeon.co/essays/why-intellectual-.thesis: Fraser challenges the claim that intellectual humility is a universal virtue; intellectual dispositions must be evaluated in the context of inquiry.
https://aeon.co/essays/why-intellectual-.argument: The same confidence that makes someone resistant to criticism can also sustain a researcher through prolonged opposition when evidence supports an unconventional finding. A trait cannot be praised without regard to circumstances and epistemic results.
https://aeon.co/essays/why-intellectual-.intellectual_background: Virtue epistemology examines traits that contribute to good thinking. Fraser questions whether there is a universal list of intellectual virtues independent of situation.
https://aeon.co/essays/why-intellectual-.example: Barbara McClintock persisted with unconventional genetic research despite resistance. Persistence was useful partly because her evidence was good, not simply because she was stubborn.
https://aeon.co/essays/why-intellectual-.strongest_objection: Humility may be valuable as a general safeguard even if exceptional confidence sometimes succeeds.
https://aeon.co/essays/why-intellectual-.possible_response: A general tendency can be useful without being universally virtuous; what matters is whether a disposition helps someone track evidence in that case.
https://aeon.co/essays/why-intellectual-.implications: Institutions should reward revision in response to evidence and principled persistence, rather than praising a single personality trait.
